comment: Exam predictions for physics, derived ONLY from the three school papers 2023-2025, the topic tests, their mark schemes and the examiner reports. Each item now carries mustKnow (the exact content, in the wording the mark scheme wants) and practice (questions with mark-scheme answers) so the page is revisable on its own.
basis: The school's 2023, 2024 and 2025 end-of-year papers, the Y10 topic tests, their mark schemes and the department's examiner reports.
caveat: It reads the pattern of three papers and the department’s own reports. Use it to order your revision, never to skip a topic. The resit paper can ask anything on the specification.

paperShape.given: An equation sheet on the reverse of the front page. Seventeen equations are NOT on it — those must be memorised.
notes: One minute per mark. A 13-mark question is 13 minutes, not 25.
Every paper carries at least one full practical/data question and at least one graph to plot or read.
Turn every page — in 2025 several students missed a 15-mark question at the back.

bands.title: Nailed on
bands.note: In all three papers. These are where the marks live — learn the wording, not just the topic.

items.claim: Static electricity — the four sentences the department marks hardest
items.why: Every paper, and the bluntest examiner report in the pack.

mustKnow.gist: RUB THING = ELECTRON JUMP ACROSS. THING THAT TAKE = MINUS. THING THAT LOSE = PLUS. PROTON NEVER MOVE.
mustKnow.exact: Charging by friction: friction transfers ELECTRONS from one material to the other. The one that GAINS electrons becomes negative; the one that LOSES them is left positive. Protons never move.

mustKnow.gist: BOTH THING END WITH SAME SIZE CHARGE. ONE PLUS, ONE MINUS.
mustKnow.exact: The two objects always end up with EQUAL AND OPPOSITE charges, because charge is conserved.

mustKnow.gist: EARTH = SAY WHERE ELECTRON GO. "ELECTRON FLOW TO EARTH." NOT JUST "IT SAFE".
mustKnow.exact: Earthing: you must say WHERE the electrons go — "electrons flow to earth (through a conductor) so charge cannot build up". Saying "it is earthed so it is safe" scores zero: it repeats the question.

mustKnow.gist: CHARGED STICK PULL PLAIN THING. NEAR SIDE GO OPPOSITE. ALWAYS PULL, EITHER WAY.
mustKnow.exact: A charged rod attracts an UNCHARGED object because it INDUCES an opposite charge on the near side. The object stays uncharged overall, and is attracted whichever sign the rod is.

mustKnow.gist: PLASTIC = CHARGE STUCK WHERE PUT. METAL IN HAND = CHARGE RUN AWAY.
mustKnow.exact: Conductor vs insulator: on an insulator charge stays where it was put; on an earthed or handheld metal it flows away instantly, so no charge builds up.

mustKnow.gist: DETECTOR NAME = GOLD-LEAF ELECTROSCOPE. LEAF RISE BECAUSE SAME CHARGE PUSH APART.
mustKnow.exact: The detector is the GOLD-LEAF ELECTROSCOPE — learn the name, it is in the spec and a mark was deducted for not knowing it. The leaf rises because leaf and stem carry the SAME charge and like charges repel.

mustKnow.gist: NEVER SAY MAGNET. MAGNET WORD = ALL MARK DEAD.
mustKnow.exact: Never write magnet, magnetic or magnetised in this topic — 2025: "any mention of magnets or electromagnetic force automatically lost all marks".

practice.q: A student rubs a balloon on a jumper. The balloon becomes negatively charged. Explain how, and state the charge on the jumper.
practice.a: Friction transfers electrons 1; electrons move FROM the jumper TO the balloon, so the balloon gains electrons 1; the jumper is left positive, equal and opposite, because charge is conserved 1.

practice.q: Explain why connecting an earthing wire to an aircraft makes refuelling safe.
practice.a: The wire is a conductor providing a path to earth 1; electrons flow to earth 1; so charge cannot build up to the point where a spark jumps and ignites the fuel vapour 1. "It is earthed so it is safe" scores 0.

practice.q: A charged rod is brought near a thin stream of uncharged water. Explain why the stream bends towards the rod.
practice.a: The rod repels/attracts the electrons in the water, so charge is INDUCED — the near side gains the opposite charge 1; the water stays uncharged overall 1; the near side is closer so the attraction beats the repulsion and the stream bends towards the rod 1. Never say the water is charged or repelled.

items.claim: The practical/data question: variables, validity, best-fit line
items.why: 56 marks across three papers — the second-biggest topic on the paper, and mostly wording rather than physics.

mustKnow.gist: YOU CHANGE = INDEPENDENT. YOU MEASURE = DEPENDENT. YOU KEEP SAME = CONTROL. NAME THEM. "FAIR TEST" = NOTHING.
mustKnow.exact: INDEPENDENT variable = the one you change. DEPENDENT = the one you measure. CONTROL = the ones you keep the same. Name the actual variables — "make it a fair test" scores nothing.

mustKnow.gist: NOT "DO AGAIN". SAY: DO THREE TIME, TAKE MEAN.
mustKnow.exact: Instead of "repeat the experiment": repeat each measurement three times and calculate a MEAN.

mustKnow.gist: NOT "BE MORE ACCURATE". NAME BETTER TOOL AND WHY. MICROMETER READ 0.01 MM.
mustKnow.exact: Instead of "be more accurate": name a finer instrument and why — e.g. a micrometer instead of a ruler, because it reads to 0.01 mm.

mustKnow.gist: NOT "MORE READING". SAY: MORE VALUES, WIDER RANGE.
mustKnow.exact: Instead of "take more readings": take readings at more values of the independent variable, across a wider range.

mustKnow.gist: PRECISE = CLOSE TOGETHER. ACCURATE = CLOSE TO TRUTH. TIGHT BUT WRONG = ZERO ERROR.
mustKnow.exact: PRECISE = readings close together. ACCURATE = close to the true value. Tight but wrong = a systematic error (e.g. a zero error).

mustKnow.gist: WEIRD POINT: NAME IT, KEEP IN TABLE, LEAVE OUT OF MEAN, IGNORE FOR LINE.
mustKnow.exact: Anomalies: identify it, leave it in the table, EXCLUDE it from the mean and ignore it when drawing the line.

mustKnow.gist: GRAPH: YOU-CHANGE ON BOTTOM. LABEL AXIS + UNIT. ONE SMOOTH LINE, NOT FUZZY.
mustKnow.exact: Graphs: independent on the x-axis, both axes labelled with quantity AND unit, plots to the nearest gridline, ONE smooth best-fit line (not sketchy or feathery), through the origin only if the data says so.

mustKnow.gist: LEAVE YOUR LINES ON GRAPH. LINES = MARKS.
mustKnow.exact: Always leave your construction lines on the graph when you read a value — they carry marks of their own.

practice.q: A student investigates how the extension of a spring depends on the force applied. State the independent, dependent and one control variable.
practice.a: Independent: the force/weight added 1. Dependent: the extension of the spring 1. Control: the same spring / same starting length / same temperature 1.

practice.q: A student's five readings are 4.2, 4.4, 4.3, 7.9 and 4.3 cm. Explain what they should do with these results.
practice.a: Identify 7.9 as an anomaly 1; exclude it from the mean, so the mean is (4.2+4.4+4.3+4.3)/4 = 4.3 cm 1. Leave it in the table but ignore it when drawing the line.

practice.q: Suggest two ways the student could improve the accuracy of their measurements of a wire's diameter.
practice.a: Use a micrometer rather than a ruler, because it reads to a finer resolution (0.01 mm) 1; measure at several points along the wire and take a mean 1. "Be more careful" and "be more accurate" score nothing.

items.claim: Particles, gases and thermal — the biggest topic on the paper
items.why: 65 marks across three papers, more than forces. Mostly particle explanations plus two calculations.

mustKnow.gist: SOLID = NEAT, WOBBLE IN PLACE. LIQUID = CLOSE, MESSY, SLIDE. GAS = FAR, FAST, ALL DIRECTION.
mustKnow.exact: Particle arrangement — SOLID: regularly packed, vibrating about fixed positions. LIQUID: close together, irregular, sliding past each other. GAS: far apart, random, fast, in all directions.

mustKnow.gist: MELT = ENERGY IN, BOND BREAK, NEAT GO MESSY. TEMPERATURE STAY SAME — ENERGY BREAK BOND, NOT HEAT UP.
mustKnow.exact: Melting: energy in, bonds between particles WEAKEN or break, particles go from regular to irregular and from vibrating to sliding. Temperature stays CONSTANT during a change of state because the energy goes into breaking bonds, not raising temperature.

mustKnow.gist: GAS PRESSURE = PARTICLE HIT WALL. HIT = FORCE. FORCE PER AREA = PRESSURE. SAME ON ALL WALL.
mustKnow.exact: Gas pressure is caused by particles COLLIDING WITH THE WALLS; each collision exerts a force, and force per unit area is pressure. It acts equally on all walls because the particles move randomly in all directions.

mustKnow.gist: HOT GAS, SAME BOX: PARTICLE FASTER, HIT WALL MORE OFTEN AND HARDER. PRESSURE UP.
mustKnow.exact: Heating a gas at constant volume: particles gain kinetic energy → collide with the walls MORE FREQUENTLY and with MORE FORCE → pressure rises.

mustKnow.gist: GAS LAW = USE KELVIN. K = °C + 273. COLDEST EVER = −273 °C.
mustKnow.exact: ALWAYS convert to kelvin for gas laws: K = °C + 273. Absolute zero is −273 °C, found by extrapolating a pressure–temperature graph BACK to zero pressure.

mustKnow.gist: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (SAME TEMP). p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂ (SAME BOX, KELVIN ONLY).
mustKnow.exact: p₁V₁ = p₂V₂ (Boyle, constant temperature) · p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂ (pressure law, constant volume, kelvin only).

mustKnow.gist: ρ = m ÷ V (MASS, NOT WEIGHT). p = F ÷ A. LIQUID p = hρg — DEEP MATTER, SHAPE NOT.
mustKnow.exact: Density ρ = m ÷ V — uses MASS not weight. Pressure p = F ÷ A. Pressure in a liquid p = h × ρ × g, which depends on DEPTH only, not on the shape or width of the container.

mustKnow.gist: E = mcΔθ. MEASURE IT: V AND I GIVE POWER, TIME IT, E = VIt, WEIGH IT, c = E ÷ (mΔθ).
mustKnow.exact: Specific heat capacity: E = m × c × Δθ. To measure it: use an ammeter and voltmeter to find power, measure the temperature rise AND the time, find E = VIt, measure the mass on a balance, then c = E ÷ (mΔθ).

practice.q: Explain, in terms of particles, why the pressure of a gas in a sealed rigid container increases when it is heated.
practice.a: The particles gain kinetic energy / move faster 1; they collide with the walls more frequently 1; and collide with more force, so the average force (and therefore pressure) increases 1.

practice.q: A gas at 8.2 kPa and 1200 K is cooled to 1600 K at constant volume. Calculate the new pressure.
practice.a: Use p₁/T₁ = p₂/T₂ 1; 8.2/1200 = p₂/1600 1; p₂ = 11 kPa 1. Temperatures must be in kelvin.

practice.q: A substance is heated at constant power. Explain why its temperature stays constant while it melts.
practice.a: The energy supplied is used to weaken/break the bonds between particles 1; rather than to increase the kinetic energy of the particles, so the temperature does not rise 1.

practice.q: Calculate the energy needed to raise 1.2 kg of a substance (c = 840 J/kg°C) from 10 °C to 37 °C.
practice.a: Δθ = 37 − 10 = 27 °C 1; E = mcΔθ = 1.2 × 840 × 27 1; = 27 000 J 1.

items.claim: A circuits question: V = IR plus a component investigation
items.why: Every paper — a filament lamp, thermistor, LDR or diode, plus meter placement and current at a junction.

mustKnow.gist: AMMETER IN LINE. VOLTMETER ACROSS. SWAP THEM = LOSE MARK EVERY TIME.
mustKnow.exact: AMMETER in series (the current flows through it). VOLTMETER in parallel, across the component. Getting these the wrong way round is a guaranteed lost mark.

mustKnow.gist: SERIES: SAME CURRENT, VOLTAGE SPLIT, R ADD UP. PARALLEL: SAME VOLTAGE, CURRENT SPLIT, R SMALLER THAN SMALLEST.
mustKnow.exact: SERIES: current is the same everywhere, voltage splits between components, resistances add (R = R₁ + R₂). PARALLEL: voltage is the same across each branch, current splits, total resistance is LESS than the smallest branch.

mustKnow.gist: CURRENT IN = CURRENT OUT AT JUNCTION.
mustKnow.exact: Current is CONSERVED at a junction — what goes in equals what comes out (16 + 19 = 35 mA).

mustKnow.gist: V = IR · Q = It (SECONDS) · P = IV · E = IVt. TURN mA INTO A FIRST.
mustKnow.exact: V = IR · Q = It (time in SECONDS) · P = IV · E = IVt. Convert mA to A before substituting: the topic test capped answers at 2 marks for not doing it.

mustKnow.gist: LAMP: HOTTER WIRE = MORE RESISTANCE. ELECTRON BUMP LATTICE MORE.
mustKnow.exact: FILAMENT LAMP: as voltage rises the current rises less steeply — resistance INCREASES because the filament's temperature increases, so there are more interactions between electrons and the lattice.

mustKnow.gist: THERMISTOR: HOT = LESS RESISTANCE. LDR: BRIGHT = LESS RESISTANCE.
mustKnow.exact: THERMISTOR: resistance DECREASES as temperature increases (non-linear). LDR: resistance decreases as light increases.

mustKnow.gist: TEST CIRCUIT: CELL + AMMETER IN LINE + VOLTMETER ACROSS + WAY TO CHANGE VOLTAGE. WORTH 4 MARK ALONE.
mustKnow.exact: To investigate a component: cell + ammeter in series + voltmeter in parallel + a variable power supply or rheostat to vary the voltage. That circuit is worth 4 marks on its own.

mustKnow.gist: TAKE PART OUT AND LEAVE GAP: RESISTANCE UP, CURRENT DOWN.
mustKnow.exact: If a component is removed leaving a break, total resistance increases (or there are fewer paths), so the current decreases.

practice.q: A thermistor has 0.59 V across it and a current of 0.0062 A. State the formula linking voltage, current and resistance, then calculate its resistance.
practice.a: voltage = current × resistance 1; substitution 0.59 = 0.0062 × R 1; rearrangement R = 0.59/0.0062 1; R = 95 Ω 1.

practice.q: Explain how the reading on a voltmeter across a thermistor changes when the room gets colder.
practice.a: The voltmeter reading increases 1; because the resistance OF THE THERMISTOR increases as temperature falls 1; so it takes a greater share of the supply voltage / the current in the circuit decreases 1.

practice.q: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the voltage across it increases.
practice.a: Resistance increases as voltage increases 1; because the temperature of the filament increases, so there are more interactions/collisions between the electrons and the lattice ions 1.

practice.q: Two resistors are in series across a 12 V supply with a current of 0.016 A. One is 250 Ω. Calculate the other.
practice.a: Total resistance = V/I = 12/0.016 = 750 Ω 1; resistances in series add 1; R = 750 − 250 = 500 Ω 1.

items.why: In all three papers, and the topic test adds fission/fusion detail.

mustKnow.gist: ALPHA = HELIUM NUCLEUS, 2 PROTON 2 NEUTRON. BETA = FAST ELECTRON FROM NUCLEUS. GAMMA = WAVE, NO MASS NO CHARGE.
mustKnow.exact: ALPHA = a helium NUCLEUS, 2 protons + 2 neutrons. BETA = a fast electron from the nucleus (a neutron becomes a proton). GAMMA = an electromagnetic wave, no mass or charge.

mustKnow.gist: ALPHA STOP BY PAPER. BETA BY ALUMINIUM. GAMMA NEED THICK LEAD. MOST IONISING = ALPHA. BIG IONISE ALWAYS = SMALL PENETRATE.
mustKnow.exact: Penetration: alpha stopped by paper/few cm of air; beta by a few mm of aluminium; gamma only reduced by thick lead or concrete. Most ionising = alpha (and least penetrating — the two always go together).

mustKnow.gist: ALPHA: MASS −4, ATOMIC −2. BETA: MASS SAME, ATOMIC +1. GAMMA: NOTHING CHANGE.
mustKnow.exact: Decay changes: ALPHA mass −4, atomic −2. BETA mass unchanged, atomic +1. GAMMA both unchanged. Example: ²³⁵₉₂U → ²³¹₉₀Th + ⁴₂α.

mustKnow.gist: HALF-LIFE = TIME FOR HALF THE LEFTOVER TO DECAY. ALWAYS SAME. HEAT NOT CHANGE IT.
mustKnow.exact: HALF-LIFE = the time for half the remaining undecayed nuclei to decay (or for the activity to halve). Constant for an isotope; unaffected by temperature or chemistry.

mustKnow.gist: ON GRAPH: HALVE THE START, READ ACROSS THEN DOWN. SHOW LINES. THREE HALF-LIFE = ÷2 THREE TIME.
mustKnow.exact: Read half-life off a graph by halving the starting activity and reading across, then down — and SHOW those lines. Three half-lives means ÷2 three times: 800 → 400 → 200 → 100.

mustKnow.gist: BACKGROUND = RADON FROM ROCK, SPACE RAY, FOOD, BRICK. TAKE BACKGROUND AWAY FIRST.
mustKnow.exact: BACKGROUND radiation comes mostly from natural sources — radon from rocks, cosmic rays, food, building materials. Always SUBTRACT background from a count rate before analysing.

mustKnow.gist: ISOTOPE = SAME PROTON, DIFFERENT NEUTRON. ACTIVITY IN BECQUEREL.
mustKnow.exact: ISOTOPES: same number of protons, different number of neutrons. Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq).

mustKnow.gist: FISSION = BIG ONE SPLIT. FUSION = TWO SMALL JOIN. FUSION NEED BIG HEAT AND PRESSURE, NUCLEUS PUSH APART.
mustKnow.exact: FISSION is the SPLITTING of a large nucleus; FUSION is the JOINING of two small nuclei. Fusion needs very high temperature and pressure because nuclei repel and need enough energy to get close enough.

practice.q: A source has an activity of 8000 Bq and a half-life of 5.6 years. Calculate its activity after 16.8 years.
practice.a: 16.8 ÷ 5.6 = 3 half-lives 1; 8000 → 4000 → 2000 → 1000 Bq 1.

practice.q: Complete: ²³⁵₉₂U → ²³¹...Th + ...₂α
practice.a: Bottom number on Th = 90 1; top number on α = 4 1. Alpha decay: mass −4, atomic −2.

practice.q: State two differences between alpha and beta radiation.
practice.a: Any two: alpha is a helium nucleus / beta is an electron 1; alpha is more ionising than beta 1; alpha is less penetrating (stopped by paper) than beta (stopped by aluminium) 1; alpha has more mass / moves more slowly 1.

practice.q: Explain the difference between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
practice.a: Fission is the SPLITTING of a large nucleus into smaller nuclei 1; fusion is the JOINING of two small nuclei to form a larger nucleus 1.

items.claim: Waves: v = fλ with a unit conversion built in
items.why: Every paper, and the conversion is deliberate — the reports call these POT (power-of-ten) errors.

mustKnow.gist: v = fλ. CHANGE UNIT FIRST. 40 kHz MEAN 40 000 Hz.
mustKnow.exact: v = f × λ. Convert first: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz, 1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz. A 40 kHz question means 40 000 Hz.

mustKnow.gist: TRANSVERSE = WOBBLE SIDEWAYS (LIGHT). LONGITUDINAL = WOBBLE ALONG (SOUND).
mustKnow.exact: TRANSVERSE: vibrations perpendicular to the direction of travel (light, water, all EM waves). LONGITUDINAL: vibrations parallel to travel (sound).

mustKnow.gist: LONG TO SHORT: RADIO, MICRO, INFRARED, VISIBLE, UV, X-RAY, GAMMA. LONG WAVE = LOW FREQUENCY.
mustKnow.exact: EM spectrum in order, longest wavelength to shortest: RADIO, MICROWAVE, INFRARED, VISIBLE, ULTRAVIOLET, X-RAY, GAMMA. Longest wavelength = lowest frequency.

mustKnow.gist: USE: RADIO TALK · MICRO COOK+PHONE · INFRARED REMOTE+HEAT PICTURE · VISIBLE SEE+FIBRE · UV MARK+SUNBED · X-RAY BONE · GAMMA KILL GERM+CANCER.
mustKnow.exact: Uses: radio — broadcasting; microwave — cooking and mobile/satellite signals; infrared — remote controls, thermal imaging, grills; visible — sight, optical fibres; UV — security marking, sun beds; X-ray — bone imaging; gamma — sterilising, treating cancer.

mustKnow.gist: HARM: MICRO COOK INSIDE · INFRARED BURN SKIN · UV SKIN CANCER+EYE · X-RAY AND GAMMA IONISE, MAKE CANCER.
mustKnow.exact: Dangers: microwaves heat internal tissue; infrared burns skin; UV damages surface cells and causes skin cancer and eye damage; X-rays and gamma are ionising and can mutate cells causing cancer.

mustKnow.gist: ECHO GO THERE AND BACK. DISTANCE TO THING = HALF. FORGET HALF = LOSE MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Echo/sonar questions: the pulse travels there AND BACK, so the distance to the object is HALF the total. Forgetting to halve is the standard error.

mustKnow.gist: REFLECT: ANGLE IN = ANGLE OUT. MEASURE FROM NORMAL, NEVER FROM SURFACE.
mustKnow.exact: Reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the NORMAL (the perpendicular), never from the surface.

mustKnow.gist: GO INTO THICK STUFF: SLOW, BEND TOWARD NORMAL. COME OUT: FAST, BEND AWAY. FREQUENCY NEVER CHANGE.
mustKnow.exact: Refraction: entering a denser medium (air → glass) the wave SLOWS and bends TOWARDS the normal; leaving it speeds up and bends away. The frequency never changes.

practice.q: A sound wave has a frequency of 40 kHz and travels at 1500 m/s in water. Calculate its wavelength.
practice.a: Convert: 40 kHz = 40 000 Hz 1; λ = v/f = 1500/40 000 1; = 0.0375 m (3.75 cm) 1.

practice.q: A sonar pulse returns after 0.4 s. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in water. Calculate the depth of the seabed.
practice.a: Total distance = 1500 × 0.4 = 600 m 1; the pulse travels there and back 1; depth = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 m 1.

practice.q: State one use and one danger of ultraviolet radiation.
practice.a: Use: security marking / sun beds / detecting forged notes / sterilising water 1. Danger: damages surface cells, causing skin cancer and eye damage 1.

bands.title: Very likely
bands.note: Twice in three years, or flagged hard by the reports.

items.claim: Hooke's law and a spring investigation
items.why: Two of three papers, and 2025's biggest question (15 marks) was built on it.

mustKnow.gist: PULL TWICE HARD = STRETCH TWICE FAR. STRAIGHT LINE THROUGH ZERO.
mustKnow.exact: Hooke's law: extension is DIRECTLY PROPORTIONAL to the force applied — a straight line through the ORIGIN on a force–extension graph.

mustKnow.gist: EXTENSION = NEW LENGTH − OLD LENGTH. NOT THE WHOLE LENGTH.
mustKnow.exact: EXTENSION = stretched length − original length. Never plot the total length.

mustKnow.gist: LINE STOP AT LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY. AFTER THAT: CURVE, SPRING MAY STAY BENT.
mustKnow.exact: The straight line stops at the LIMIT OF PROPORTIONALITY; beyond it the graph curves and the spring may not return to its original length (it deforms inelastically).

mustKnow.gist: ELASTIC = GO BACK TO OLD SHAPE WHEN YOU LET GO.
mustKnow.exact: ELASTIC behaviour = the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed.

mustKnow.gist: F = kx. k = SPRING CONSTANT IN N/m = GRADIENT OF GRAPH.
mustKnow.exact: F = k × x, where k is the spring constant in N/m — the gradient of the force–extension graph.

mustKnow.gist: ENERGY IN STRETCHED SPRING = AREA UNDER FORCE–EXTENSION GRAPH.
mustKnow.exact: Energy stored in a stretched spring comes from the work done stretching it, and is the AREA under the force–extension graph.

practice.q: A spring extends 4.0 cm when a force of 2.0 N is applied. Calculate the spring constant in N/m.
practice.a: Convert: 4.0 cm = 0.040 m 1; k = F/x = 2.0/0.040 1; k = 50 N/m 1.

practice.q: Explain what is meant by the limit of proportionality on a force–extension graph.
practice.a: The point beyond which extension is no longer directly proportional to force 1; the graph stops being a straight line and begins to curve 1.

items.claim: Moments and the principle of moments

mustKnow.gist: MOMENT = FORCE × PERPENDICULAR DISTANCE FROM PIVOT. UNIT N m. NOT DISTANCE MOVED — THAT WORK.
mustKnow.exact: Moment = force × PERPENDICULAR distance from the pivot, in newton metres (N m). Not 'distance moved' — that is work.

mustKnow.gist: BALANCED: CLOCKWISE MOMENT = ANTICLOCKWISE MOMENT.
mustKnow.exact: PRINCIPLE OF MOMENTS: for a balanced object, total clockwise moments = total anticlockwise moments.

mustKnow.gist: F₁d₁ = F₂d₂ ACROSS PIVOT. THAT THE SEE-SAW SUM.
mustKnow.exact: So F₁ × d₁ = F₂ × d₂ across the pivot — the standard see-saw calculation.

mustKnow.gist: TURN DISTANCE INTO METRE FIRST. CHECK WHICH SIDE EACH FORCE ON.
mustKnow.exact: Convert distances to metres before calculating, and check which forces act on which side of the pivot.

practice.q: A 3.0 N weight sits 0.40 m to the left of a pivot. A second weight sits 0.24 m to the right and the beam balances. Calculate that weight.
practice.a: Principle of moments: clockwise = anticlockwise 1; 3.0 × 0.40 = F × 0.24 1; F = 1.2/0.24 = 5.0 N 1.

items.why: Energy is in all three papers, usually as efficiency or conservation. The wording is marked exactly.

mustKnow.gist: EFFICIENCY = USEFUL OUT ÷ TOTAL IN × 100. DROP "USEFUL" OR "TOTAL" = LOSE MARK. NEVER OVER 100%.
mustKnow.exact: efficiency = (USEFUL energy output ÷ TOTAL energy input) × 100. Dropping either 'useful' or 'total' loses the mark. Efficiency can never exceed 100%.

mustKnow.gist: ENERGY NEVER MADE, NEVER GONE. ONLY MOVE. "LOST" MEAN WENT TO HEAT.
mustKnow.exact: Energy is CONSERVED — never created or destroyed, only transferred between stores. 'Energy is lost' means transferred to a less useful store, usually heating the surroundings.

mustKnow.gist: STORES: KINETIC, GRAVITY, ELASTIC, THERMAL, CHEMICAL, NUCLEAR, ELECTROSTATIC, MAGNETIC.
mustKnow.exact: The energy stores: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, nuclear, electrostatic, magnetic.

mustKnow.gist: GPE = mgh (h = HEIGHT CHANGE). KE = ½mv². SPEED IS SQUARED — TWICE SPEED = FOUR TIME ENERGY.
mustKnow.exact: GPE = m × g × h (h is the CHANGE IN HEIGHT). KE = ½ × m × v² — the speed is SQUARED, so doubling speed quadruples the energy.

mustKnow.gist: W = Fd, DISTANCE ALONG THE FORCE. P = E ÷ t, IN WATT (1 W = 1 J/s).
mustKnow.exact: Work done W = F × d, distance moved IN THE DIRECTION OF THE FORCE. Power P = E ÷ t, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s).

mustKnow.gist: SANKEY: ARROW WIDTH = ENERGY. WIDTH GOING OUT MUST ADD UP TO WIDTH GOING IN.
mustKnow.exact: Sankey diagram: arrow WIDTH is proportional to energy, and the widths out must total the width in.

mustKnow.gist: QUESTION SAY "IN TERMS OF FORCES" = TALK FORCE (WEIGHT, AIR RESISTANCE, RESULTANT). NOT ENERGY.
mustKnow.exact: A falling object question asked 'in terms of forces' must be answered with forces (weight, air resistance, resultant) — NOT energy. 2025 penalised energy answers here.

practice.q: A motor is supplied with 500 J and does 150 J of useful work. Calculate its efficiency.
practice.a: efficiency = (useful output ÷ total input) × 100 1; = (150/500) × 100 = 30% 1.

practice.q: A 2.0 kg ball is dropped from 5.0 m (g = 10 N/kg). Calculate its speed just before it lands, assuming no air resistance.
practice.a: GPE = mgh = 2.0 × 10 × 5.0 = 100 J 1; all GPE becomes KE, so ½mv² = 100, giving v² = 2 × 100 ÷ 2.0 = 100 1; v = 10 m/s 1.

practice.q: Explain, in terms of forces, why a falling object reaches terminal velocity.
practice.a: At first weight is greater than air resistance, so there is a resultant downward force and it accelerates 1; as speed increases, air resistance increases 1; when air resistance equals weight the resultant force is zero, so it travels at constant (terminal) velocity 1. Do not mention energy.

items.claim: Specific heat capacity or an E = IVt calculation
items.why: An electrical-heating experiment turned into a calculation — 2024 as SHC, 2025 as E = IVt.

mustKnow.gist: E = mcΔθ. JOULE, kg, J/kg°C, AND Δθ = TEMP CHANGE (END − START).
mustKnow.exact: E = m × c × Δθ — energy in joules, mass in kg, c in J/kg°C, Δθ the TEMPERATURE CHANGE (final − initial).

mustKnow.gist: ELECTRIC ENERGY IN: E = IVt. TIME IN SECONDS.
mustKnow.exact: Electrical energy supplied: E = I × V × t, with time in SECONDS.

mustKnow.gist: WHOLE EXPERIMENT: V AND I GIVE POWER, TIME THE HEATING, E = IVt, WEIGH IT, c = E ÷ (mΔθ).
mustKnow.exact: Combining them is the whole experiment: measure V and I to get power, time the heating, find E = IVt, weigh the substance, then c = E ÷ (mΔθ).

mustKnow.gist: WHY c COME OUT TOO BIG: HEAT ESCAPE TO ROOM, SO YOU COUNT MORE ENERGY THAN WENT IN. WRAP THE BLOCK.
mustKnow.exact: Why the measured c comes out too HIGH: energy is lost to the surroundings, so more energy is recorded than actually went into the substance. Insulate the block to reduce it.

mustKnow.gist: Δθ IS A DIFFERENCE — SAME NUMBER IN °C OR K. BUT GAS LAW STILL NEED KELVIN.
mustKnow.exact: Δθ is a DIFFERENCE, so it is the same number in °C or K — but absolute temperatures in gas laws must be in kelvin.

practice.q: A 50 W heater warms 0.50 kg of aluminium (c = 900 J/kg°C) for 3.0 minutes. Calculate the temperature rise.
practice.a: t = 3.0 × 60 = 180 s 1; E = Pt = 50 × 180 = 9000 J 1; rearrange Δθ = E/(mc) = 9000/(0.50 × 900) 1; Δθ = 20 °C 1.

practice.q: Suggest why the value of specific heat capacity found in this experiment is higher than the true value.
practice.a: Some energy is transferred to the surroundings rather than to the block 1; so the energy recorded is greater than the energy that actually raised the block's temperature, making c appear larger 1.

items.claim: Q = It with an answer in standard form
items.why: The 2024 electroscope question, and the report's complaint about power-of-ten errors.

mustKnow.gist: Q = It. COULOMB, AMP, SECONDS. MINUTE MUST BE CHANGED.
mustKnow.exact: Q = I × t — charge in coulombs, current in amps, time in SECONDS. Minutes must be converted.

mustKnow.gist: FLIP IT: I = Q ÷ t, AND t = Q ÷ I.
mustKnow.exact: Rearranged: I = Q ÷ t and t = Q ÷ I.

mustKnow.gist: TINY ANSWER STAY IN STANDARD FORM. 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 15 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ A.
mustKnow.exact: Small answers stay in standard form: 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 15 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ A. The 2025 report begged for standard form and flagged 'far too many POT errors'.

mustKnow.gist: PREFIX: mA = ×10⁻³, µA = ×10⁻⁶, nC = ×10⁻⁹.
mustKnow.exact: Watch the prefixes: mA = ×10⁻³, µA = ×10⁻⁶, nC = ×10⁻⁹.

practice.q: A charge of 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ C is transferred in 15 s. Calculate the current. Give your answer in standard form.
practice.a: State Q = It or I = Q/t 1; I = 6.0 × 10⁻⁸ ÷ 15 1; I = 4.0 × 10⁻⁹ A 1.

practice.q: A current of 250 mA flows for 2.0 minutes. Calculate the charge transferred.
practice.a: Convert: 250 mA = 0.25 A and 2.0 min = 120 s 1; Q = It = 0.25 × 120 1; Q = 30 C 1.

bands.title: Due a return
bands.note: On the specification but thin or missing in the last three papers — worth an hour each.

items.why: The motion GRAPHS have been light, though the equations appear. Cheap marks if asked.
items.evidence: 2024 Q8 used the equations; the graphs themselves have been rare

mustKnow.gist: DISTANCE–TIME: GRADIENT = SPEED. FLAT = STOPPED. STEEP = FAST. CURVE = SPEED CHANGING.
mustKnow.exact: DISTANCE–TIME graph: the GRADIENT is the SPEED. Flat line = stationary. Steeper = faster. A curve means the speed is changing.

mustKnow.gist: VELOCITY–TIME: GRADIENT = ACCELERATION. AREA UNDER LINE = DISTANCE.
mustKnow.exact: VELOCITY–TIME graph: the GRADIENT is the ACCELERATION, and the AREA UNDER the line is the DISTANCE travelled.

mustKnow.gist: TRIANGLE AREA = ½ × BASE × HEIGHT. THAT HOW YOU GET BRAKING DISTANCE.
mustKnow.exact: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height — that is how a braking distance is found from a v–t graph.

mustKnow.gist: GRADIENT GOING DOWN = SLOWING. DO NOT GIVE A PLUS ANSWER.
mustKnow.exact: A negative gradient on a v–t graph is deceleration; the mark scheme rejects a positive answer when the object is slowing.

mustKnow.gist: v = u + at · v² = u² + 2as · a = (v − u) ÷ t. a USE CHANGE IN VELOCITY. NOT a = v/t.
mustKnow.exact: The suvat equations: v = u + at · v² = u² + 2as · a = (v − u) ÷ t. Note a = CHANGE in velocity ÷ time — the topic test explicitly rejects a = v/t.

mustKnow.gist: STOPPING = THINKING + BRAKING. THINKING GO WITH SPEED. BRAKING GO WITH SPEED SQUARED — GROW MUCH FASTER.
mustKnow.exact: Stopping distance = THINKING distance + BRAKING distance. Thinking distance is directly proportional to speed; braking distance is proportional to speed SQUARED, so it grows much faster.

mustKnow.gist: TIRED, DRINK, DISTRACTED = THINKING DISTANCE ONLY. BRAKING NOT CHANGE.
mustKnow.exact: Tiredness, alcohol and distraction increase THINKING distance only — they have no effect on braking distance.

practice.q: A car decelerates from 30 m/s to rest in 6.2 s. Calculate the acceleration, and the distance travelled while braking.
practice.a: a = change in velocity ÷ time = (−)30/6.2 1; = (−)4.8 m/s² 1. Distance = area under the v–t line 1; = ½ × 30 × 6.2 1; = 93 m 1.

practice.q: Explain the effect of tiredness on thinking distance and on braking distance.
practice.a: Thinking distance increases 1; because reaction time increases 1. Braking distance is unaffected 1; because it does not depend on human factors — only on speed, brakes, tyres and road conditions 1.

practice.q: State what the gradient of a distance–time graph represents, and what the area under a velocity–time graph represents.
practice.a: Gradient of a distance–time graph = speed 1; area under a velocity–time graph = distance travelled 1.

items.claim: Refraction and reflection with a ray diagram
items.why: The waves questions have leaned on v = fλ rather than ray optics. A diagram-labelling question is overdue.

mustKnow.gist: NORMAL = LINE AT 90° TO SURFACE WHERE RAY HIT. ALL ANGLE FROM NORMAL. THAT IS THE MARK.
mustKnow.exact: The NORMAL is the line drawn at 90° to the surface at the point where the ray hits. ALL angles are measured from the normal, never from the surface — that is the labelling mark.

mustKnow.gist: REFLECT: ANGLE IN = ANGLE OUT.
mustKnow.exact: Law of reflection: angle of incidence = angle of reflection.

mustKnow.gist: INTO THICK STUFF (AIR → GLASS): SLOW DOWN, BEND TOWARD NORMAL.
mustKnow.exact: Refraction into a DENSER medium (air → glass or water): the wave slows down and bends TOWARDS the normal.

mustKnow.gist: INTO THIN STUFF (GLASS → AIR): SPEED UP, BEND AWAY FROM NORMAL.
mustKnow.exact: Refraction into a LESS dense medium (glass → air): the wave speeds up and bends AWAY from the normal.

mustKnow.gist: FREQUENCY NEVER CHANGE. SPEED AND WAVELENGTH CHANGE TOGETHER.
mustKnow.exact: The frequency NEVER changes on refraction — the speed and the wavelength change together.

mustKnow.gist: LABEL: NORMAL DASHED, RAY IN WITH ARROW, ANGLE i, AND RAY OUT WITH ITS ANGLE.
mustKnow.exact: Label a ray diagram with: the normal (dashed), the incident ray with an arrow, the angle of incidence i, and the refracted or reflected ray with its angle.

practice.q: A ray of light passes from air into a glass block. Describe what happens to its speed and direction, and explain why the frequency is unchanged.
practice.a: It slows down 1; it bends towards the normal 1; the frequency is set by the source and does not change — the wavelength changes with the speed so that v = fλ still holds 1.

practice.q: A ray hits a mirror at 30° to the mirror surface. State the angle of reflection.
practice.a: The angle of incidence is measured from the NORMAL, so it is 90 − 30 = 60° 1; angle of reflection = 60° 1.

bands.title: The marks thrown away regardless of topic
bands.note: The department's own list. Worth 5–10 marks a paper on their figures.

items.claim: If it says "state the formula", write the formula
items.why: A free mark asked almost every year, skipped by people who dive into the arithmetic.

mustKnow.gist: WRITE EQUATION BEFORE PUTTING NUMBER IN. THAT IS ITS OWN MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Write the equation in words or symbols BEFORE substituting — it is a separate mark from the answer.

mustKnow.gist: ANY REARRANGE FINE. V = IR, R = V/I, I = V/R ALL SCORE.
mustKnow.exact: Standard symbols and rearrangements are accepted (V = IR, R = V/I, I = V/R all score).

mustKnow.gist: 17 EQUATION NOT ON SHEET. LEARN THEM. LIST ON EXAM REFERENCE PAGE.
mustKnow.exact: The 17 equations NOT on the formula sheet must be memorised — check the Exam reference page for the list.

mustKnow.gist: CANNOT FINISH SUM? STILL WRITE FORMULA AND NUMBERS. BANK THE MARK.
mustKnow.exact: Even if you cannot finish the calculation, writing the formula and the substitution banks marks.

practice.q: Why does writing 'voltage = current × resistance' before calculating earn a mark on its own?
practice.a: Because the mark scheme awards a separate mark for stating the formula, independently of the substitution and the final answer 1.

items.claim: Convert units BEFORE substituting, and check the unit demanded
items.why: POT (power-of-ten) errors are the biggest single arithmetic loss across all three reports.

mustKnow.gist: kHz→Hz ×1000 · MHz→Hz ×10⁶ · min→s ×60 · hour→s ×3600 · g→kg ÷1000 · cm→m ÷100 · mA→A ÷1000 · cm³→m³ ÷10⁶.
mustKnow.exact: kHz → Hz (×1000) · MHz → Hz (×10⁶) · minutes → seconds (×60) · hours → seconds (×3600) · g → kg (÷1000) · cm → m (÷100) · mA → A (÷1000) · cm³ → m³ (÷10⁶).

mustKnow.gist: READ THE ANSWER LINE FIRST. IT TELL YOU THE UNIT, SOMETIME THE SIG FIG.
mustKnow.exact: Read the ANSWER LINE before you calculate — it names the unit you must give, and sometimes the number of significant figures.

mustKnow.gist: BIG AND TINY NUMBER STAY IN STANDARD FORM. 4.8 × 10⁶, NOT 4 800 000.
mustKnow.exact: Large and small numbers stay in standard form: 4.8 × 10⁶, not 4 800 000.

mustKnow.gist: MARK OFTEN JUST FOR THE UNIT. WRITE cm³/min, NOT cm³/m.
mustKnow.exact: A mark is often awarded purely for the correct unit — and cm³/m (metres) instead of cm³/min has cost marks in this department.

practice.q: A student writes 'rate = 3 cm/m'. Give two things wrong with this unit.
practice.a: It should be cm³ (a volume), not cm 1; 'm' means metres — minutes is 'min' 1.

items.claim: Show every step — substitution and rearrangement earn marks
items.why: A wrong final answer with correct working still scores; a wrong answer alone scores zero.

mustKnow.gist: MARK SCHEME = SUBSTITUTION 1, REARRANGE 1, ANSWER 1. THREE SEPARATE MARK.
mustKnow.exact: The standard calculation mark scheme is: substitution [1], rearrangement [1], evaluation [1]. Three separate marks.

mustKnow.gist: ECF: EARLY MISTAKE COST ONE MARK ONLY — BUT ONLY IF WORKING IS ON THE PAGE.
mustKnow.exact: ECF (error carried forward) means a mistake early on costs ONE mark, not the whole question — but only if your working is on the page.

mustKnow.gist: RIGHT ANSWER NO WORKING = USUALLY FULL MARK. WRONG ANSWER NO WORKING = ZERO.
mustKnow.exact: A correct answer with no working usually scores full marks; a wrong answer with no working scores nothing.

mustKnow.gist: ROUND AT THE END ONLY, TO THE SIG FIG THE QUESTION ASK FOR.
mustKnow.exact: Round only at the END, and to the number of significant figures the question asks for.

practice.q: You substitute correctly but make an arithmetic slip in the final step of a 3-mark calculation. How many marks can you still score?
practice.a: 2 of 3 — the substitution and rearrangement marks stand, and ECF applies to later parts, provided the working is shown 1.
